name: Carmine
poem: Harvested from the cochineal insect of the cactus — a red so prized that Spain guarded its source as a state secret.

recipe.note: A deep, cool crimson red shaded with the faintest black.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: The deepest, coolest red available to European painters for three hundred years — and a colour that funded the Spanish Empire.

entries.title: The Family of Charles IV
entries.blurb: The royal family's velvets and silks are painted in glazes of pure carmine — the same insect-derived pigment that filled the royal coffers shipping it from Mexico.

entries.title: Girl with a Red Hat
entries.blurb: The hat's saturated red is built up in thin glazes of carmine over a vermilion underlayer — Vermeer's technique for a red that glows from within.
entries.imageCredit: National Gallery of Art DC · PD

entries.title: Mexican Codices
entries.blurb: Aztec painters used cochineal-derived carmine for thousands of years before European contact — a knowledge the conquistadors immediately weaponised.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: The most expensive red ever traded — and the colour of every garment that needed to mean authority or sex.

entries.title: The Cardinal's Cap
entries.blurb: Cardinal's red is by ancient tradition exactly the carmine of dried cochineal — a colour that said, in the medieval imagination, blood ready to be shed.

entries.title: The Red Sole
entries.blurb: Louboutin painted his prototype's sole with red nail polish to make it pop — the carmine sole is now a trademark defended in courts on three continents.

entries.title: Flamenco Costume
entries.blurb: The traje de flamenca's reds are intensified by the lining beneath — every twirl flashes carmine. The colour is older than the dance.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Carmine is built one tiny insect at a time — and the supply chain has barely changed in five centuries.

entries.title: The Cochineal Beetle
entries.blurb: The females live on prickly pear cacti, feeding on the sap. Scraped off, dried, and crushed, 70,000 of them yield one pound of dye.

entries.title: The Prickly Pear Cactus
entries.blurb: Native to Mexico, deliberately exported worldwide to support the cochineal industry — every Mediterranean hillside with prickly pear is part of the dye trail.

entries.title: The Red Rose
entries.blurb: Carmine is the colour the Apothecary's Rose reaches for at full bloom — a coincidence the rose breeders of the 13th century enthusiastically exploited.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: Carmine never went out of fashion — but its source quietly migrated from oil paintings to lipsticks and yogurt.

entries.title: E120
entries.blurb: The same cochineal-derived carmine that coloured Renaissance velvets now tints strawberry yogurt, red lollipops, and (until 2012) Starbucks frappuccinos.

entries.title: Lipstick
entries.blurb: Carmine remains the preferred red pigment in premium lipstick — it stays brilliant on the lip and doesn't fade with sun exposure the way synthetics do.

entries.title: Campbell's Soup Cans
entries.blurb: The exact red of the Campbell's label is a synthetic carmine — chosen for its appetite-stimulating warmth, weaponised by Warhol into Pop Art's signature hue.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: The colour's name carries the insect with it — and the insect carries the colour's history.

entries.title: "Kermes"
entries.blurb: The original Mediterranean red, made from a related scale insect — "kermes" gives us both "carmine" and "crimson," same root, different shade.

entries.title: "Cochineal"
entries.blurb: The Spanish word for the Mexican insect — a diminutive of "pig" (cochino), perhaps from the insect's shape, perhaps from the smell of the dye vat.

entries.title: "Nocheztli"
entries.blurb: The Aztec name for cochineal — a more accurate description than the colonial ones. The conquistadors learned the production but kept the colonial name.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Carmine is the colour blood is supposed to be — venous, not arterial — and it carries every cultural meaning blood does.

entries.title: Sacrifice
entries.blurb: Carmine is the colour of the Crucifixion in Renaissance painting and the colour of the bull's blood in Mithraic mosaics — a colour religion finds hard to avoid.

entries.title: Romance
entries.blurb: Valentine's Day, the red rose, the red dress — all carmine. The colour signals desire across cultures, with surprisingly little variation.

entries.title: Communism
entries.blurb: The Bolshevik red was carmine before it was anything else — the same colour worn by cardinals, kings, and the working class flag of revolution.
